title: Detection of Gather Victim Identity Information
shortTitle: Detection of Gather Victim Identity Information
summary: This detection strategy addresses the reconnaissance technique of gathering victim identity information, where an adversary collects employee names, email addresses, job titles, and phone numbers before an intrusion begins. It matters because these details power convincing phishing and password reset fraud, yet the collection usually happens outside the monitored estate on public sources. The telemetry that makes detection possible is web server and reverse proxy logging, identity provider sign in and failed authentication records, email gateway logs for directory style messages, and mail or web content inspection events. The main failure mode is that public collection generates no telemetry at all, so the rule can only catch the on premises or cloud side of the activity.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for signs that someone is collecting names and contact details about the people in your company. That list often includes full names, work email addresses, and job titles. The rule watches your own systems for the fast, repeated lookups that such collection creates.
beginner.whyItMatters: A short list of real names makes a fake email much easier to believe. An attacker who knows your coworkers can pretend to be one of them. If you catch the lookups, you can warn the staff whose details were taken. It also gives you an early warning before a phishing wave starts.
howItWorks: The SIEM, short for security information and event management system, stores web and identity logs in one place.
The web server access log shows every request, including the ones that fail.
The rule counts requests to staff listing pages and directory pages from a single internet address.
It also counts failed sign ins where many different real accounts are tried in a short time.
The email gateway records messages that ask staff to confirm their own details.
When one source hits many names quickly, the rule raises an alert for the analyst to review.
beginner.example: Picture a hospital sign in sheet at the front desk. One visitor who arrives and asks for the names of thirty doctors in ten minutes is unusual. A visitor who asks for one doctor is normal. The sheet gives you the visitor details, and the pattern of many names from one visitor is what draws attention.
takeaways: Identity collection often happens before any sign of a real intrusion appears.
Fast and repeated lookups of many employee records from one source are the main signal.
Public collection leaves no logs, so the rule only covers activity that touches your systems.

objectives: Describe what victim identity information means and how attackers use it.
Identify which logs can show employee detail collection inside your estate.
Build a rule that counts directory lookups from a single source.
Distinguish normal onboarding or marketing lookups from hostile collection.
Point out the coverage gap that public data collection creates.
dataSources: Web server and reverse proxy access logs recording request paths, status codes, source address and user agent
Identity provider sign in logs recording failed authentication attempts with the attempted user principal name
Email security gateway logs showing inbound directory harvest or address confirmation messages
Windows Security event 4625 account logon failure records on internal directory services
logic: The pattern is a high count of employee related lookups or failed authentications from one source over a short window. The fields to correlate are the source address, the request path or response code, the count of distinct employee names or addresses touched, and the time window. The malicious case is one external source walking a staff directory, guessing mail addresses, or trying many real user names, with no prior relationship to the site. The benign case is a recruitment drive, a sales tool, or a monitoring service that reads a known public page at a steady, low rate and stays inside documented paths.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Employee Directory Enumeration From a Single Source
# logsource:
#   product: network
#   service: http
# detection:
#   selection:
#     cs-method: 'GET'
#     cs-uri-stem|contains:
#       - '/staff'
#       - '/directory'
#       - '/people'
#   filter_known:
#     c-ip|contains: '10[.]0[.]'
#   condition: selection and not filter_known | count(c-ip) by c-ip > 30 within 10m
# level: medium
falsePositives: Recruiters and sales teams running automated contact lookups through approved business tools
Employee onboarding portals that validate new hire addresses in bulk on the first working day
Uptime and security scanning services that crawl a fixed list of public staff pages at a steady rate
tuningNotes: Baseline normal request rates to staff pages for two weeks, then set the threshold above the busiest legitimate day and add a filter for the user agents and source ranges of approved services. Scope the rule to internet facing web and identity systems rather than internal intranets. Keep failed sign in counting in its own rule so that password spray noise does not mask directory harvesting. The coverage you lose is slow, low volume collection that stays under the threshold, so keep a monthly review of distinct source addresses that touch many employee records over time.
